stories.title: A study in Science finds the next glacial period had already begun about 2,000 years ago, until warming reversed it in the 1960s
paragraphs: Two thousand years ago, the last Arctic remnant of North America's once-vast Laurentide Ice Sheet started to grow again, marking the start of a new glacial period, according to a study published in the journal Science and described by Columbia University's Climate School on Oct. 22. By the 1960s, summer temperatures had risen enough that the ice began to shrink. "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen, and yet it stopped," said Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and the study's first author.

The Laurentide covered much of Canada and the northern United States from about 95,000 to 20,000 years ago, stretching at its largest from above the Arctic Circle to Illinois. Its last vestige survives as the Barnes Ice Cap, a Delaware-sized ice cap on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada. Columbia notes that we technically still live in an ice age that began about 34 million years ago, and that what people casually call an "ice age" is a colder glacial period; the last one ended about 11,700 years ago.

The Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to its bedrock and does not slide, so it preserves plants that grew when it was small and were later buried as it expanded. Dating that vegetation with carbon-14, and, as ScienceAlert reported on Oct. 31, measuring beryllium-10 in exposed rock, the team found the ice reached its smallest size about 3,000 years ago and began re-expanding about 2,000 years ago. Columbia says previous model-based studies had suggested the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

Since about 1960 the ice cap has lost more ice each summer than it gains in winter, and ScienceAlert reports the researchers found those losses "can be almost entirely explained by rising summer temperatures." According to models of its future, the ice cap will melt completely within the next few centuries. "That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young said.

stories.title: Mistral releases the open weights of Mistral Large 4, a 1-trillion-parameter model it calls the best open model for coding
paragraphs: Mistral AI released the weights of Mistral Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, on Oct. 29, 2026, the company announced. Mistral describes it as its flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, first released in public preview earlier in October, and says it was trained from scratch on European infrastructure. The model is free to use, modify, fine-tune and commercialize under a modified MIT license, except that companies offering it as a hosted model service need a separate commercial license.

Mistral says three more weeks of reinforcement learning since the preview made Mistral Large 4 the best open-weight model for coding. It reports a lead score of 19.7% on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark and 41% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, up 13 percentage points from the preview. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral reports a 48% score, effectively tied with GLM-5.3 while using 47% fewer tokens per task; a Hugging Face post on the release lists 49.8% for the same index.

Mistral is pitching the model for defensive cybersecurity. The company reports a 51% score on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and an average 96.6% refusal rate on malicious cyber requests, the highest it measured among open models. Hugging Face's post says the model scores 82% on that index's task of reproducing and then patching a real vulnerability. Mistral also wrote that, after watching live traffic since the preview, it sees a potential for the model to help with real attacks and is changing its guardrails.

According to Hugging Face, the model is a mixture-of-experts design with a 1-million-token context window, released in FP8 and NVFP4 versions with day-one support in Transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. Mistral lists API pricing of $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens, and says the model is also available through Microsoft Foundry and NVIDIA-hosted endpoints.

stories.title: A hijacked version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension was served through Cursor's extension marketplace for about 11 hours
paragraphs: Cursor, which makes AI-assisted coding tools, published a security notice saying that maliciously modified versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension, Anthropic.claude-code versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS, were available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace between about 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. PT on Oct. 29, 2026. Cursor said these versions were not developed by Anthropic and that the incident does not affect other extensions in its marketplace. Ars Technica reported on Oct. 30 that the compromise affected at most 5,000 users, according to Cursor, and that the malicious version was distributed through Anthropic's official account on Cursor.

According to Cursor, the extension collected host and user details such as hostname, username, operating system, environment variable names, configured Git email and public IP address, added an attacker-controlled SSH key, tried to enable the local SSH service and open a reverse SSH tunnel, and set up persistence through a LaunchAgent on macOS or a scheduled task on Windows. Cursor said that, because of errors in the malicious code and because turning on SSH needs administrator rights, the tunnel step would fail on most machines, but that the key, the persistence and the host-detail report still went through.

Cursor said it removed the malicious version as soon as it was detected, shut down the whole marketplace as a precaution, audited access and found no other tampered extensions, rotated its keys, rebuilt the marketplace and brought it back online. It also said it worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker's server offline. Ars Technica reported that, as of its story, neither Cursor nor Anthropic had explained how the attackers got control of the account, and that Anthropic had not yet issued a public notice to customers.

Cursor's notice tells anyone who installed or updated to those versions in that window to check their SSH authorized_keys file for a key labeled svc-telemetry, and gives remediation scripts for macOS and Windows. It warns that uninstalling the extension may not be enough, because the payload leaves standalone persistence scripts, and advises rotating credentials and sessions reachable from affected machines. Ars Technica's report described the affected version as 2.1.313 and said the code was written for Windows, macOS and Linux; Cursor's notice, updated Oct. 30 at 11:30 a.m. PT, lists versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS.

stories.title: DeepSeek open-sources dsh-superagent, a research prototype of a coding agent that waits to be asked and splits work into parallel sessions
paragraphs: DeepSeek published a public GitHub repository, deepseek-ai/dsh-superagent-prototype, on Oct. 31, 2026, under the MIT license. The README describes dsh-superagent as a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub and, optionally, the Feishu chat app, and when someone who is allowed asks it for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person.

The README labels the code a research prototype for reference only and not an official DeepSeek product. It says much of the engineering was done by coding agents, that it may still contain bugs, and that it differs from DeepSeek's internal version and from the design described in its post Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System, some of which is not implemented. The stated principle is to take as little human attention as possible and give as much value as possible, so the agent acts only when asked or when a rule the team wrote allows it.

MarkTechPost reported on Nov. 1 that the design uses two layers: a long-running Router that handles interaction and dispatch, and isolated Worker sessions that do the work, one per work item, which the project calls a Ticket. It reported that unrequested work is gated by three modes, off, observe and auto, with observe as the default, in which the agent only records what it would have accepted. MarkTechPost listed the requirements as Node.js 22.19 or newer, git, Python, tmux and the GitHub command-line tool, and noted that the agent runs with full access as the operating-system user, so it advised isolating it before use.

Citing a Chinese tech outlet's account of DeepSeek's report, MarkTechPost said that in a simulation with about 300 messages per run, about 20 of them real work requests, the super-agent reached a 95th-percentile task completion time of 15.7 minutes, against 29.5 minutes for a single-session agent with subagents. MarkTechPost noted that these figures are self-reported, came from tests with synthetic messages and simulated tools, and that real coding quality was not measured.

stories.title: NASA asks companies how they could boost, upgrade or safely retire Hubble, as Swift falls toward re-entry after a failed boost
paragraphs: NASA issued a Request for Information on Oct. 29 to learn what industry can offer for in-space servicing of the Hubble Space Telescope, the agency announced on Oct. 30. According to NASA, it wants to hear from companies interested in boosting Hubble to a higher altitude to extend its science lifetime, servicing the telescope to enhance its capabilities, or carrying out a safe, controlled re-entry or orbital disposal at the end of its mission. Responses are due by 3 p.m. EST on Monday, Nov. 30.

"Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in the announcement. NASA science chief Nicky Fox said commercial industry has rapidly developed new capabilities for capturing and servicing satellites in space, and that the agency wants to explore ways to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while it develops the flagship mission to follow.

NASA says Hubble's altitude is slowly dropping because of atmospheric drag, the telescope has no propulsion system of its own, and analysis predicts it is likely to re-enter the atmosphere in the 2033 to 2034 timeframe. As a result, the agency expects that any mission would need to take place by 2032.

Another NASA observatory shows what happens when a boost doesn't work out. Science News reported on Oct. 30 that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, launched in 2004 to study gamma-ray bursts, is falling uncontrollably and is destined to burn up in Earth's atmosphere within days. A spacecraft NASA commissioned to lift Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August technical issues made a boost attempt impossible, according to Science News. Swift has lost about half its original altitude, a decline sped up by high solar activity, and Science News says nothing is lined up to replace its combination of instruments.

stories.title: Two different kinds of gamma-ray bursts erupted four minutes apart, a pairing astronomers had never seen
paragraphs: Astronomers have described a gamma-ray burst event unlike any other yet observed or predicted, ScienceAlert reported Oct. 30, 2026: a short burst and a long burst arriving only about four minutes apart. The event, named GRB 160425A, is described in a paper published in Nature Astronomy. According to ScienceAlert, short gamma-ray bursts last under two seconds and are thought to come from mergers of compact objects such as neutron stars and black holes, while long bursts last more than two seconds and are typically associated with the core-collapse supernovae of very massive dying stars.

The bursts were detected on April 25, 2016, by NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, and ground-based telescopes then followed the fading afterglow, ScienceAlert reports. The host galaxy, possibly a pair of merging galaxies, is so distant that the light took roughly 5.5 billion years to reach Earth. The first burst, called G1, lasted 1.7 seconds and is associated with a merger origin; the second, G2, lasted 51.2 seconds and is associated with a collapsing-star origin. Setting aside the fact that such bursts release energy in focused beams, ScienceAlert says the second burst released roughly three times as much energy as the first.

"This is so far the only event with such a strange property," corresponding author Bing Zhang, an astrophysicist at the University of Hong Kong, told ScienceAlert. "I'd think that these are two independent GRBs, but the chance of having them happen together (in the same direction and around the same time) is so low [that] we have to admit that the pair has the same origin."

According to ScienceAlert, the researchers lay out five possible explanations and call each of them challenging. Two unrelated bursts lining up by chance has odds of about 2 in a trillion for any one moment and patch of sky, or roughly 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 10 million across all of Swift's years of observing, and two bursts from different spots in the same galaxy is even less likely. A single merger burst with a tail, or a single collapsing star with a weaker precursor, both fit poorly with the long quiet gap and the energies involved. The fifth option is a single system of undetermined makeup that produced both. "All the scenarios have severe difficulties," Zhang said.
